title: Reshuffling & Draw Pile Recycling
summary: When the draw pile empties, recycle the discard pile — preserving the top card so play continues seamlessly. Practise array slicing, randomness, and the `randomize()` call.

lessons.title: Reshuffle, Preserving the Top Card
lessons.bodyMarkdown:
# Reshuffling the Discard Pile

When the draw deck runs out mid-match, Kadi recycles the discard pile into a fresh draw deck — **except** the top card, which stays in place so the next player still has something to match against.

```gdscript
func reshuffle_if_empty() -> void:
    if GameState.deck.size() > 0:
        return
    if GameState.discard_pile.size() <= 1:
        return  # nothing to recycle
    var top_card: CardData = GameState.discard_pile.pop_back()
    GameState.deck = GameState.discard_pile.duplicate()
    GameState.deck.shuffle()
    GameState.discard_pile = [top_card]
    randomize()
```

`pop_back()` lifts the top card off the discard pile. `duplicate()` makes a shallow copy of the remaining pile — important, because assigning `GameState.deck = GameState.discard_pile` would alias the same array and corrupt both. `shuffle()` randomises in place; `randomize()` reseeds the RNG so each reshuffle differs.

The two early returns are **guard clauses**: bail out if there is nothing to do. Guard clauses keep the happy path unindented and readable.

> [!WHY]
> Preserving the top card is what makes the recycle invisible to the player. If you shuffled the whole discard pile, the top of the pile would jump to a random card mid-turn, breaking whatever rule (penalty, question, jump) was in force. Slicing the top off before shuffling is a one-line fix that keeps the match continuous. The `duplicate()` call avoids aliasing — a bug where editing `deck` later would silently mutate `discard_pile` and vice versa, which is fiendish to debug.

Always `duplicate()` arrays you intend to reassign; aliasing is the source of half the array bugs in card games.

codeSnippets.caption: Recycle the discard pile, preserving the top card.

practicePrompt.instructions: Modify reshuffle_if_empty to also emit a signal `pile_recycled(new_deck_size: int)` after the shuffle. Declare the signal at the top.
practicePrompt.hint: Declare `signal pile_recycled(new_deck_size: int)` and call `.emit()` after the shuffle.
practicePrompt.solutionCode:

# ... after GameState.deck.shuffle():
pile_recycled.emit(GameState.deck.size())

quizQuestions.prompt: Why call `duplicate()` instead of assigning `GameState.deck = GameState.discard_pile`?
choices: Plain assignment would alias the same array, so mutating deck would also mutate discard_pile (and vice versa)
quizQuestions.explanation: Without duplicate, both variables point at the same underlying array. Edits to one silently affect the other — a classic source of card-game bugs.

quizQuestions.prompt: Why preserve the top card of the discard pile during reshuffle?
choices: So the next player still has a card to match against — the rule in force (penalty, question, jump) continues uninterrupted
quizQuestions.explanation: Removing the top card would change the active rule mid-turn. Keeping it makes the recycle transparent to gameplay.

lessons.title: Testing Edge Cases
lessons.bodyMarkdown:
# Testing Edge Cases

The reshuffle function *looks* correct — but "looks correct" has ended more Kadi matches than bad luck ever has. The nastiest moment to get it wrong is **mid-penalty**: a Joker demands five cards, the deck empties after two, and the recycle must fire seamlessly so the remaining three can still be drawn. We will not hope; we will test.

A test in Godot can be a plain function that builds a known state, calls the code under test, and checks the outcome with `assert()`. An assert takes a condition and an optional message; if the condition is false in a debug build, the game stops right there and shows you the message.

```gdscript
func test_reshuffle_mid_penalty() -> void:
    GameState.deck = [make_card("Clubs", 9), make_card("Hearts", 4)]
    GameState.discard_pile = build_pile_of(10)
    var expected_top: CardData = GameState.discard_pile.back()
    print("before: deck=%d discard=%d" % [GameState.deck.size(), GameState.discard_pile.size()])
    draw_cards(GameState.current_player, 5)  # Joker penalty empties the deck mid-draw
    print("after: deck=%d discard=%d" % [GameState.deck.size(), GameState.discard_pile.size()])
    assert(GameState.discard_pile.size() == 1, "discard must keep exactly the top card")
    assert(GameState.discard_pile.back() == expected_top, "top card must survive the reshuffle")
    assert(hand_size(GameState.current_player) >= 5, "all 5 penalty cards must be drawn")
```

The recipe is always the same: **arrange** a tiny, hand-built state (a two-card deck, a ten-card discard pile), **act** by triggering the edge case, **assert** on every property that must hold. The `print()` lines are cheap print-debugging — when an assert fires, the before/after sizes in the Output panel tell you instantly whether the recycle ran at all.

Note that `assert()` only runs in debug builds; exported release builds strip it entirely. That makes asserts free to sprinkle generously — they cost nothing in the shipped game — but it also means they are a development tool, not a substitute for handling real runtime errors.

While we are hunting edge cases, remember the rulebook's quiet one: **a player cannot win while any player is cardless**. It deserves the same treatment — arrange a state where an opponent holds zero cards, act by playing a would-be winning move, and assert that `has_won()` returns false.

> [!WHY]
> Edge cases like an empty deck mid-penalty happen maybe once in fifty matches — far too rarely to find by playtesting, and exactly often enough to enrage real players. A test function makes the rare case happen on demand, every single run. Simulating the improbable cheaply is the entire point of automated testing: you compress fifty matches of bad luck into one function call.

Run your test functions from a debug keybinding or a `_ready()` in a test scene, and re-run them after every change to the deck code.

codeSnippets.code:
func test_no_win_while_opponent_cardless() -> void:
    GameState.hands[1] = []  # opponent is cardless
    GameState.hands[0] = [make_card("Hearts", 7)]
    GameState.niko_declared[0] = true
    play_card(0, GameState.hands[0][0])
    assert(not has_won(0), "cannot win while any player is cardless")
codeSnippets.caption: The cardless-opponent rule gets its own test.

practicePrompt.instructions: Write `test_reshuffle_skipped_when_pile_tiny()` that sets an empty deck and a ONE-card discard pile, calls reshuffle_if_empty(), and asserts both piles are unchanged (deck still 0, discard still 1).
practicePrompt.hint: The guard clause `if GameState.discard_pile.size() <= 1: return` should make the function a no-op. Assert both sizes afterwards.
practicePrompt.solutionCode:
func test_reshuffle_skipped_when_pile_tiny() -> void:
    GameState.deck = []
    GameState.discard_pile = [make_card("Spades", 9)]
    reshuffle_if_empty()
    assert(GameState.deck.size() == 0, "deck must stay empty")
    assert(GameState.discard_pile.size() == 1, "discard must keep its single card")

quizQuestions.prompt: What happens to `assert()` calls in an exported release build of a Godot game?
choices: They crash the game on failure
They are stripped out entirely — asserts run only in debug builds
quizQuestions.explanation: Godot removes asserts from release exports, so they cost nothing in the shipped game. Use them freely during development, but never for handling real runtime errors.

quizQuestions.prompt: Why write a test function for the empty-deck-mid-penalty scenario instead of relying on playtesting?
choices: The edge case occurs too rarely to hit reliably by playing; a test makes the rare state happen on demand, every run
Tests make the game run faster
quizQuestions.explanation: Automated tests compress dozens of matches of bad luck into one repeatable function call — the improbable becomes routine, and regressions surface immediately.
